analysis.one_liner: Bans race-based preferences in federal contracting, employment, and federally funded college admissions.
analysis.headline: Introduced January 23, 2025 and sent to four House committees, the bill has taken no further action despite 9 Republican cosponsors and none from the other party.
analysis.plain_summary: The FAIR Act would bar the federal government from discriminating for or against anyone based on race, color, or national origin in contracting, hiring, and federal programs, and would bar states and private groups receiving federal money from using race in contracts, hiring, or college admissions. It defines a forbidden "preference" to include quotas, set-asides, numerical goals, and timetables, and it lets any person harmed sue in court and collect attorney's fees if they win. In practice, it would end federal programs that direct contracting work or admissions advantages toward members of specific racial or ethnic groups.
analysis.who_benefits: People who believe race-conscious federal programs have cost them a contract, a job, or a college admission, because they could sue and recover attorney's fees. Federal contractors also gain by shedding diversity-related compliance requirements.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Applicants and contractors opposing race preferences

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the federal government, its officers and employees from discriminating against or granting preference based on race, color, or national origin in federal contracts, employment, and other federal programs.
Bars states and private entities receiving federal financial assistance from using race-based preferences in contracts, employment, or college admissions.
Gives anyone harmed a private right of action to sue violators, including government entities, for relief such as back pay, with reasonable attorney's fees awarded to prevailing plaintiffs.
Requires every federal agency within 6 months of enactment to review and revise its policies and regulations to comply, and report the results to the House and Senate Judiciary Committees.

analysis.who_pays: Minority-owned businesses that rely on federal contracting set-asides, students whose admissions or aid considers race, universities and employers that would face new lawsuits, and agencies that would have to rewrite their programs within six months.
analysis.who_pays_short: Minority contractors, universities, and federal agencies

drawbacks.text: The bill's definition of preference covers quotas, set-asides, numerical goals, and timetables, which would eliminate programs that steer federal contracting work to minority-owned businesses and similar race-conscious efforts.

The private right of action against violators, including government entities and schools, could produce substantial litigation against employers, universities, and state agencies over what counts as a preference.

By barring both discrimination and preference by race, the bill removes the tools federal policy has used to counteract discrimination against specific groups, a cost its critics emphasize; its supporters counter that equal treatment under the law is the point.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers what its supporters promise — a single, enforceable rule of race-neutral treatment across federal contracting, hiring, and education, with a court remedy for individuals — but its real cost falls on the specific people and businesses current race-conscious programs were built to reach, and it shifts disputes over fairness from agency policy into individual lawsuits.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on January 23, 2025 and sent to four House committees, and no committee has acted on it since, so it simply sits waiting with no hearing or vote scheduled.

narrative.text: Representative Thomas Tiffany introduced the FAIR Act of 2025 in the House on January 23, 2025.
On introduction it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and additionally to the Oversight and Government Reform, Education and Workforce, and House Administration committees.
Nine representatives cosponsored the bill, all Republicans, and no action beyond the initial referrals appears in the record.
Federal law and agency programs on race-conscious contracting, hiring, and admissions remain unchanged while the bill waits in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one yet: because no committee or chamber has acted, current federal programs and rules are exactly as they were before the bill was introduced, so supporters of the change have gained nothing and opponents have lost nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; status quo stands

for.name: Reps. Owens, Tenney, Hageman, Ogles, Miller of Illinois, Grothman, Weber of Texas, and Moore of Alabama
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 9 cosponsors are Republicans, and no Democrat appears among the bill's supporters in the record.

industries.industry: Minority-owned federal contractors and set-aside programs
industries.note: The bill defines preference to include quotas, set-asides, and numerical goals, ending programs that steer federal contract work to minority-owned businesses. These owners would bear the direct cost of the change.

industries.industry: Federal contractors and recipients of federal licenses and aid
industries.note: Contractors, licensees, and aid recipients gain by shedding requirements to pursue diversity goals in contracting, hiring, and admissions, reducing compliance obligations and litigation exposure from those requirements.

Institutions receiving federal aid could no longer use race in admissions, and would face a new private right of action from applicants. Some already operate under court limits on race-conscious admissions, so the practical change varies by school.
Agencies and contractors would have to strip race-based goals from policies within six months, shrinking the market for programs built around those targets.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has sat with four committees since January 2025 with no hearing, markup, or vote, and has no Democratic support. Most referred bills never reach the floor, and unless a committee schedules action this bill will likely die when this Congress ends in early 2027.
